simulator_description: The simulator models a single-stage Beer Game inventory system where, at each discrete time step, on-hand inventory is adjusted by incoming pipeline arrivals (shipments with stochastic lead times), customer demand is sampled stochastically and fulfilled from inventory with unmet demand accumulating as nonnegative backlog, and a new replenishment order (either provided or a base-stock fallback) is added into the pipeline with optional quantity noise. The state is represented compactly as {inventory, backlog, pipeline as (quantity, remaining lead time) pairs, time}, and the step function enforces sensible supply-chain invariants (no negative stocks/flows) while allowing different update conventions for arrival/demand/order timing, which captures common Beer Game bookkeeping variants. Parameters control demand level/noise, shipment noise, lead-time distribution, backlog handling, and update convention, and the simulator uses per-trajectory seeded RNGs for reproducible rollouts; an accompanying calibration module fits these parameters to observed trajectories via simulation-based inference, which is a reasonable structure for generating and matching supply-chain state trajectories under uncertainty.

This simulator generates single-stage Beer Game (SUPPLY) trajectories where a retailer-like node evolves over discrete time with nonnegative inventory, backlog (unmet demand carried forward), and a shipment pipeline represented as quantity/remaining-lead-time pairs. Each step optionally receives pipeline arrivals (counting down lead times), realizes stochastic customer demand from a count process (Poisson or overdispersed Gamma-Poisson/Negative Binomial), fulfills demand/backlog subject to inventory and a backlog-vs-demand service priority parameter, and places a replenishment order that enters the pipeline with stochastic quantity noise and a categorical lead time over 1–5 periods. A categorical “update convention” parameter randomizes the order of arrivals, fulfillment, and ordering to match different operational timing assumptions; using probabilistic choices, explicit pipeline countdown, and invariant checks (no negative stock/backlog) makes the structure consistent with standard Beer Game mechanics while keeping dynamics stochastic and identifiable for calibration.

This simulator models a single-stage Beer Game inventory system over discrete time, where each state tracks on-hand inventory, accumulated backlog, and an in-transit pipeline of placed orders with stochastic lead times. At each step, pipeline shipments age and may arrive to replenish inventory, then exogenous customer demand is sampled as a nonnegative count (Poisson with optional noise) and is fulfilled using conserved accounting (ship min(inventory, backlog+demand), with any unmet amount becoming backlog); an agent action adds to a baseline order quantity and the resulting order is added to the pipeline with a categorical lead time in {1..5}. Choosing one update convention (order vs demand timing) per trajectory and reusing it reduces unnecessary rollout variance while still allowing different plausible event-order assumptions, and the overall structure reflects standard supply-chain dynamics where arrivals, demand, and replenishment decisions jointly drive inventory and backlog trajectories.

This simulator models a single-stage Beer Game supply chain over discrete time, where the state tracks on-hand inventory, unmet demand as backlog, and a shipment pipeline represented as (quantity, remaining lead time) tuples. At each step it updates the system by (i) advancing the pipeline and adding any arrivals to inventory, (ii) sampling exogenous customer demand using an overdispersed Gamma-Poisson (negative-binomial-like) process with mild seasonality, and (iii) placing the agent’s provided order into the pipeline with a stochastic lead time drawn from a categorical distribution over 1–5 periods; three alternative within-step update conventions (arrivals/demand/order orderings) are selectable via learned logits. The accounting is conservative and standard for inventory/backlog systems—fulfillment ships up to available inventory against backlog plus new demand—while using the action directly as the order quantity (action-first) ensures trajectories reflect the external policy, and parsing true pipeline tuples (or using zero-quantity dummies when only length is known) avoids fabricating supply that would distort dynamics.

This simulator models a single-stage Beer Game supply chain where, at each discrete time step, on-hand inventory is increased by shipments arriving from an order pipeline with stochastic lead times, then reduced by fulfilling stochastic customer demand, with any unmet demand accumulating as backlog; new orders (actions) are appended to the pipeline as future shipments. The state is therefore naturally represented by (inventory, backlog, a FIFO-like list of pipeline entries with remaining lead times, and time), and the step logic conserves flow by shipping at most what is available and carrying the remainder as backlog. Demand is generated as a nonnegative count using an overdispersed (Gamma-Poisson) process with a mostly time-driven mean plus weak, bounded conditioning on current backlog and pipeline length to reduce systematic drift when calibrating from limited data, while preserving insertion order in the pipeline avoids altering queue semantics; a small set of “update conventions” (different within-step orderings of arrivals, demand, and ordering) is selected per trajectory to reflect plausible bookkeeping variations without changing the core dynamics.
